title: Interpretations Belong to God
summary: In prison Joseph interprets the dreams of Pharaoh’s butler and baker; both come true in three days, yet the restored butler forgets him.
historicalContext: Joseph had been in Egypt more than ten years when two of Pharaoh’s highest household officers joined him in custody; two years after this chapter he stands before Pharaoh at thirty (41:1, 46). The chief cupbearer and chief baker controlled what reached the king’s mouth, and in courts where poisoning was a real fear such men were trusted confidants with great influence. Records of Egyptian conspiracy trials show court servants of this rank investigated, some executed and some cleared. Egyptians valued dreams as messages about the future and kept trained interpreters and dream manuals, which the prisoners could not reach. Royal birthdays or accession anniversaries were marked with banquets and acts of clemency. Public exposure of an executed body on a stake was a shameful penalty, made worse in a culture that placed great weight on careful burial.
literaryContext: Genesis 40 stands between the summary of God’s blessing in the prison (39:21-23) and Joseph’s rise before Pharaoh (chapter 41). It is the second of three pairs of dreams in the Joseph story: Joseph’s own sheaves and stars (37:5-11), the two officers’ dreams here, and Pharaoh’s cows and ears of grain. The chapter is built with careful symmetry. Two officials offend, two dreams come in one night, each is told and interpreted in parallel form, and both are fulfilled on the third day. The number three runs through every part: branches, baskets, stages of growth, actions, and days. The idiom “lift up the head” is used three times with opposite outcomes. Joseph’s plea to be remembered (v. 14) and the butler’s failure to remember (v. 23) frame the outcome, leaving Joseph in the prison and creating the suspense that chapter 41 resolves.
themes: Faithful service in a hidden place

outline.title: Pharaoh’s Officers in Joseph’s Prison
outline.summary: The king’s butler and baker offend him and are placed in the prison where Joseph is bound, and Joseph is appointed to serve them.

outline.title: Two Dreams and No Interpreter
outline.summary: Both officers dream on the same night; Joseph notices their sad faces, hears their trouble, and declares that interpretations belong to God.

outline.title: The Butler’s Dream and Joseph’s Plea
outline.summary: Joseph interprets the vine with three branches as restoration within three days and asks the butler to remember him before Pharaoh.

outline.title: The Baker’s Dream
outline.summary: The baker tells of three baskets and birds eating from the top one; Joseph foretells his execution within three days.

outline.title: Fulfilment and Forgetfulness
outline.summary: On Pharaoh’s birthday the butler is restored and the baker hanged, exactly as Joseph said, but the butler forgets Joseph.

verses.bibleText: And it came to pass after these things, that the butler of the king of Egypt and his baker had offended their lord the king of Egypt.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And it came to pass after these things.” The phrase marks a new scene without measuring the time between. Joseph has already risen to oversee the prison (39:22), and since he would stand before Pharaoh at thirty (41:46), roughly eleven of his thirteen years as slave and prisoner lie behind him when this episode opens. The narrator does not linger over the long, unrecorded days; he moves straight to the event God will use.

Two new figures enter: “the butler of the king of Egypt and his baker.” The English titles sound domestic, yet these were men of rank. The butler was the cupbearer who served the king his drink and was answerable for its safety; the baker supervised the bread and cakes that came to the royal table. In a court where the threat of poison was taken seriously, those who handled the king’s food and drink held his life in their hands, and with that came intimacy and influence. Nehemiah, cupbearer to Artaxerxes centuries later, could make a request of the king that changed the fortunes of Jerusalem (Nehemiah 2:1-8).

These men “had offended their lord.” The verb is the ordinary Hebrew word for sin, the very word Joseph used when he refused to “sin against God” (39:9). The contrast is deliberate. Joseph sits in prison because he refused to sin; the officers arrive because they are charged with sinning against their master. The text never names the offence, and later events suggest that only one of the two was found guilty. Speculation about a plot or a careless mistake goes beyond the narrative. What matters is that God brings to Joseph’s door a man who will one day stand at Pharaoh’s elbow.

wordNotes.explanation: A participle of the causative verb shaqah, “to give drink,” so literally “the one who gives drink,” the cupbearer. The same form is used of Nehemiah’s office at the Persian court (Nehemiah 1:11). Its partner, ’ofeh, is the ordinary word for a baker (Hosea 7:4). Both titles describe the king’s personal service, which explains their access to him and the danger they faced when he became suspicious.

The common verb for sin, meaning to miss the mark or to fail in an obligation. It can describe an offence against a human superior (1 Samuel 24:11) as well as against God. Its use here sets the officers beside Joseph, who would not “sin against God” (39:9). The butler later uses the related noun when he recalls “my faults” before Pharaoh (41:9).

verses.bibleText: And Pharaoh was wroth against two of his officers, against the chief of the butlers, and against the chief of the bakers.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And Pharaoh was wroth against two of his officers.” Their titles are now given in full: “the chief of the butlers” and “the chief of the bakers.” Each was head over a staff of servants, which makes their fall the more striking. A word from the king had made them, and a word could unmake them.

The narrator’s phrasing gives Pharaoh’s anger a clear object, whereas Potiphar’s anger in the previous chapter was stated without saying whom it targeted (39:19). The verb used for Pharaoh’s wrath is one often applied to God’s displeasure with sin (Numbers 16:22; Deuteronomy 9:19). Proverbs observes that “the king’s wrath is as messengers of death” (Proverbs 16:14), and the officers knew it. They now lived under a sentence not yet spoken.

Both men are again called by the same word that described Potiphar, “officers” (39:1). The prison now holds Pharaoh’s servants and Pharaoh’s former slave together. All three had been close to power; all three are now at the mercy of others. Only one of them, however, is there with a clear conscience and with the Lord’s presence (39:21).

wordNotes.explanation: Qatsaf describes anger that breaks out, often the indignation of a superior. It is used of Moses’ anger at Israel’s disobedience (Exodus 16:20) and frequently of God’s wrath (Deuteronomy 9:19). Pharaoh himself is again the subject in 41:10, where the butler recalls that “Pharaoh was wroth with his servants.”

verses.bibleText: And he put them in ward in the house of the captain of the guard, into the prison, the place where Joseph was bound.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And he put them in ward in the house of the captain of the guard, into the prison, the place where Joseph was bound.” Three descriptions of the location pile up: a place of custody, the captain’s house, the prison. The last phrase brings the reader’s eye back to Joseph. Of all the places in Egypt where Pharaoh might have held these men, they are sent to the one where Joseph is.

The “captain of the guard” bears the same title as Potiphar (37:36; 39:1). The text does not say outright that he is the same man, though the identical title invites the connection, and the prison seems to have been on or attached to his estate. If so, Joseph’s former master, who had imprisoned him on his wife’s word, now places the king’s officers under his care. Whether Potiphar had come to doubt the accusation, the narrator does not say; he only shows that the man in authority continued to trust Joseph.

“The place where Joseph was bound” recalls his chains. Psalm 105 remembers that Joseph’s feet were hurt with fetters and that he was laid in iron, “until the time that his word came” (Psalm 105:18-19). He had freedom of movement within the prison by now, but he remained a prisoner. The psalm’s “until” gives the right frame for this chapter. God was testing Joseph by his word and preparing the hour of release, and the arrival of these two men was the first visible movement toward it. Joseph had no way of knowing that. He saw only two more prisoners to look after.

wordNotes.explanation: Mishmar means guard or custody, a place where someone is watched and held. It describes detention awaiting a decision, as when the Israelite who gathered sticks on the Sabbath was put “in ward” until the LORD declared his sentence (Numbers 15:34). The officers are not yet condemned; their cases await Pharaoh’s judgment. Joseph’s brothers will later be held in the same kind of custody (42:17).

verses.bibleText: And the captain of the guard charged Joseph with them, and he served them: and they continued a season in ward.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And the captain of the guard charged Joseph with them, and he served them.” Two prisoners of state, whose fate was undecided and who might yet return to power, required careful handling. The captain assigned them to the man he trusted most. The keeper had already placed the whole prison in Joseph’s hand (39:22); now a specific charge from higher authority made him their personal attendant.

The verb for “served” is the same one used of Joseph’s service to Potiphar (39:4). It describes the attendance a personal servant gives to a master. The irony is plain: the men who had served Pharaoh at table are now served by a Hebrew prisoner. Joseph, whose dreams had shown his brothers bowing to him, spends his days waiting on others. The path to the throne ran through the servants’ quarters, a pattern Christ made the rule of his kingdom when he said that whoever would be chief must be servant of all (Mark 10:44-45).

“And they continued a season in ward.” The Hebrew says simply “days,” an indefinite stretch of time. Weeks or months passed while the investigation dragged on. For Joseph this was routine service. For the officers it was anxious waiting, each day possibly bringing word of release or death. That suspense explains their reaction to the dreams that follow.

wordNotes.term: וַיְשָׁרֶת אֹתָם (vayesharet ’otam) — and he served them
wordNotes.explanation: Sharat means to minister or attend, usually as a personal servant to a superior. It describes Joseph’s service to Potiphar (39:4), Joshua’s attendance on Moses (Exodus 24:13), and later the priests’ ministry in the sanctuary (Numbers 3:6). The word carries honour as well as humility: a trusted attendant stood close to the one he served.

verses.bibleText: And they dreamed a dream both of them, each man his dream in one night, each man according to the interpretation of his dream, the butler and the baker of the king of Egypt, which were bound in the prison.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And they dreamed a dream both of them, each man his dream in one night.” The verse is wordy in Hebrew, repeating “each man” and “his dream,” and the repetition presses the point that two separate men had two separate dreams on the same night. Simultaneous dreams were too striking to be coincidence. Both men sensed that something was being said to them.

The verse adds that each dream came “according to the interpretation of his dream.” Each dream already carried its own meaning, fitted to the man who dreamed it. In the other pairs of dreams in the Joseph story, two dreams share one message: the sheaves and the stars (37:5-9), and Pharaoh’s cows and ears of grain, which Joseph will say are “one” (41:25). Here the pair is split. The dreams look alike and will be interpreted alike at the start, but they end in opposite places.

The narrator again calls them “the butler and the baker of the king of Egypt, which were bound in the prison.” The full titles set their former dignity against their present condition. Men who had stood in the palace now lay in the place of the bound, and God chose that place and that night to speak to them.

Dreams in Genesis are a way God makes himself known, to the covenant family and to outsiders alike. He warned Abimelech in a dream (20:3), spoke to Laban the same way (31:24), and will speak to Pharaoh (41:1). Elihu later reflects that God speaks “in a dream, in a vision of the night,” to turn a person from his purpose (Job 33:14-16). Such dreams are always God’s initiative; the dreamer can neither summon nor decode them on his own, as the next verses will show.

wordNotes.term: אִישׁ כְּפִתְרוֹן חֲלֹמוֹ (’ish kefitron chalomo) — each man according to the interpretation of his dream
wordNotes.explanation: Pitron, “interpretation,” and the verb patar, “to interpret,” occur in the Old Testament only in the Joseph story (40:5, 8, 16, 22; 41:8-15). The phrase means that each dream was suited to its own meaning; the butler repeats the expression when he tells Pharaoh what happened (41:11). In the Aramaic of Daniel a related word, peshar, carries the same sense (Daniel 2:4).

verses.bibleText: And Joseph came in unto them in the morning, and looked upon them, and, behold, they were sad.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And Joseph came in unto them in the morning, and looked upon them, and, behold, they were sad.” Joseph’s daily round brought him to their room as usual. What he noticed was their faces. A man consumed by his own wrongs might have walked past two gloomy prisoners without a second look; in a prison, low spirits were hardly news. Joseph saw, and he cared enough to see.

The word translated “sad” describes more than mild unhappiness. It is used elsewhere of a troubled or agitated state, of a sea that rages and of a king whose face darkens with displeasure (Jonah 1:15; Proverbs 19:12). The officers were shaken. They believed their dreams concerned their fate, and the pending verdict made that fate urgent.

The narrator’s “behold” lets the reader look over Joseph’s shoulder. Years of injustice had not turned him inward. The same attentiveness that made him a good steward made him a good friend to the afflicted. The Servant of the LORD in Isaiah is one who knows how to speak a word in season to the weary (Isaiah 50:4), and Joseph, in his small way, was about to do just that.

wordNotes.explanation: From za‘af, a verb of agitation, used of a stormy sea (Jonah 1:15) and of the king’s rage (Proverbs 19:12; 2 Chronicles 26:19). Here it describes troubled, downcast faces, the outward sign of inward dread. The same word appears when Daniel’s steward fears that the young men’s faces will look “worse liking” than those of their peers (Daniel 1:10).

verses.bibleText: And he asked Pharaoh's officers that were with him in the ward of his lord's house, saying, Wherefore look ye so sadly to day?

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And he asked Pharaoh’s officers that were with him in the ward of his lord’s house, saying, Wherefore look ye so sadly to day?” The narrator once more spells out who these men are and where they are, as though to underline the strangeness of the scene. Pharaoh’s officers are “with him,” sharing Joseph’s confinement, and the place is “his lord’s house,” the household of the master who had put him there. The slave addresses the king’s men, and they answer him.

Joseph’s question is literally, “Why are your faces bad today?” The word “today” is telling. Joseph knew these men well enough to see that this morning was different from other mornings. Daily attendance had made him a student of their moods. A question like this costs little, yet it opens a door. Nehemiah’s king asked him a similar question, “Why is thy countenance sad?”, and the answer led to the rebuilding of Jerusalem (Nehemiah 2:2-5). Here the question leads, by a longer road, to the saving of Egypt and of Jacob’s family.

Suffering can shrink a person’s world to the size of his own pain. Joseph had more cause than most to be absorbed in his grievances: betrayed by his brothers, slandered by his mistress, forgotten by everyone who had once known him. Instead, he noticed others. Paul urges believers to look “not every man on his own things, but every man also on the things of others” (Philippians 2:4), and Christ embodied that mind on his way to the cross. The ministry that eventually brought Joseph out of prison began with this simple act of attention.

wordNotes.term: מַדּוּעַ פְּנֵיכֶם רָעִים הַיּוֹם (maddua‘ peneikhem ra‘im hayyom) — wherefore look ye so sadly to day?
wordNotes.explanation: Literally “Why are your faces bad today?” Ra‘, usually “evil” or “bad,” here describes a troubled appearance. Nehemiah’s king uses the same expression, asking why his cupbearer’s face is “sad” (ra‘) when he is not sick (Nehemiah 2:2). The contrast returns in verse 14, where Joseph speaks of the time when it will be “well” (yitav) with the butler.

verses.bibleText: And they said unto him, We have dreamed a dream, and there is no interpreter of it. And Joseph said unto them, Do not interpretations belong to God? tell me them, I pray you.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And they said unto him, We have dreamed a dream, and there is no interpreter of it.” Their distress lay less in the dreams than in their helplessness before them. In Egypt dreams were taken seriously as signs of what was coming, and a class of trained experts, with manuals listing dream images and their meanings, stood ready to explain them. At court such men were near at hand; Pharaoh will summon them in the next chapter (41:8). In prison there was no one. The officers had a message about their future and no means of reading it.

Joseph answered with a question: “Do not interpretations belong to God?” The sentence is short, and it carries the theology of the whole chapter. Interpretations do not belong to expertise, to manuals, or to the wise men of Egypt. They belong to God, who sends the dream and alone knows its meaning. Joseph will say the same to Pharaoh with even greater emphasis: “It is not in me: God shall give Pharaoh an answer of peace” (41:16). Daniel, facing a king whose wise men could not tell his dream, makes the identical confession: “there is a God in heaven that revealeth secrets” (Daniel 2:27-28). The ancient Greek translation catches the sense well, asking whether the explanation of dreams does not come through God.

Joseph uses the general word for God, Elohim, rather than the covenant name the narrator used in chapter 39. He speaks to Egyptians in terms they could grasp, while making clear that the God he serves is the one who governs what their dreams foretell. His confession is also a striking act of faith. Joseph’s own dreams of sheaves and stars had led, as far as anyone could see, to a pit, a slave market, and a prison. He had every reason to doubt that dreams meant anything. He still believed that God speaks and that God’s word does not fail.

“Tell me them, I pray you.” Having given God the credit, Joseph offers himself as the channel. The order matters. He claims no skill; he claims only that God can give the meaning, and that he is willing to be used. Those who serve God are stewards of gifts they did not create (1 Corinthians 4:7; 1 Peter 4:10). Joseph’s readiness to speak of God in a prison cell, to men who did not share his faith, shows that his witness did not depend on favourable surroundings. Through prophets and finally through his Son, the same God has made known what is to come (Amos 3:7; Hebrews 1:1-2), and his word remains the one sure guide to the future.

wordNotes.term: הֲלוֹא לֵאלֹהִים פִּתְרֹנִים (halo’ le’lohim pitronim) — do not interpretations belong to God?
wordNotes.explanation: A rhetorical question expecting the answer yes: interpretations are God’s possession. The preposition le marks ownership, as in “the earth is the LORD’s” (Psalm 24:1). Joseph’s claim is repeated before Pharaoh (41:16, 25, 28), and Daniel echoes it in Babylon (Daniel 2:28). The Greek Old Testament renders the line as a question about whether the explanation comes “through God.”

The participle of patar, “to interpret,” used in the Hebrew Bible only in Genesis 40–41. It names the person who explains what a dream means. Pharaoh’s court had many would-be interpreters, yet “there was none that could interpret” his dreams (41:8), and the butler later describes Joseph as the one who interpreted for him (41:12).

verses.bibleText: And the chief butler told his dream to Joseph, and said to him, In my dream, behold, a vine was before me;

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And the chief butler told his dream to Joseph.” The butler speaks first, without hesitation. His readiness may hint at an easy conscience; a man with nothing to hide is quicker to hear what his dream portends. The order also serves the story. A favourable interpretation given first will draw out the baker, who might otherwise have kept silent.

“In my dream, behold, a vine was before me.” The dream opens in the butler’s own world. Wine was produced and drunk in Egypt, as tomb paintings of harvest and pressing scenes show, and the vine was the starting point of the butler’s craft. The dream takes him back to his work, placing the source of Pharaoh’s cup right before his eyes. That alone may have given him hope, since it pictured him occupied with his duties rather than shut away from them.

The vine is a rich image in Scripture. Israel would be pictured as a vine brought out of Egypt (Psalm 80:8), and Jesus called himself “the true vine” (John 15:1). Those later uses do not need to be read back into the butler’s dream, which concerns his own restoration, but they show how naturally the vine speaks of life and fruitfulness. In this dream that sense of life sets the tone, and it will contrast sharply with the baker’s dream.

wordNotes.explanation: The common word for the grapevine, appearing here for the first time in Genesis, though Noah had already planted a vineyard (9:20). It becomes a symbol of Israel planted by God (Psalm 80:8) and of peace and plenty, each person under his vine (Micah 4:4). In the butler’s dream it simply represents the source of the king’s wine and the butler’s office.

verses.bibleText: And in the vine were three branches: and it was as though it budded, and her blossoms shot forth; and the clusters thereof brought forth ripe grapes:

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And in the vine were three branches: and it was as though it budded, and her blossoms shot forth; and the clusters thereof brought forth ripe grapes.” The dream compresses a season into moments. Buds appear, blossoms burst out, and clusters ripen, all in one continuous movement. What normally takes months happens before the dreamer’s eyes, which suits the short span of time the dream will be found to signify.

The number three, which will govern the whole chapter, appears for the first time: three branches. The growth itself also unfolds in three stages, budding, blossoming, ripening. Such patterns are part of the dream’s language, and Joseph will read them as markers of time. Three days later the outcome will confirm that reading.

The scene recalls another quick flowering in the Pentateuch. When God chose Aaron as priest, his rod “brought forth buds, and bloomed blossoms, and yielded almonds” overnight (Numbers 17:8). There, too, swift growth signalled God’s choice and favour. The butler’s vine breathes life and readiness; nothing hinders it, and the fruit is brought to its purpose. The baker’s dream will have no such movement toward completion.

wordNotes.term: הִבְשִׁילוּ אַשְׁכְּלֹתֶיהָ עֲנָבִים (hivshilu ’ashkelotheha ‘anavim) — the clusters thereof brought forth ripe grapes
wordNotes.explanation: The verb bashal in this causative form means to ripen or bring to maturity. ’Eshkol is a cluster, the word that gave the valley of Eshcol its name when the spies cut down a great bunch of grapes there (Numbers 13:23-24). The whole sentence describes a vine passing from bud to harvest without pause.

verses.bibleText: And Pharaoh's cup was in my hand: and I took the grapes, and pressed them into Pharaoh's cup, and I gave the cup into Pharaoh's hand.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And Pharaoh’s cup was in my hand: and I took the grapes, and pressed them into Pharaoh’s cup, and I gave the cup into Pharaoh’s hand.” The name of Pharaoh sounds three times in a single verse, and the cup is mentioned three times as well. The butler’s whole dream revolves around the king. He is back at his post, his hands busy with the work he had done for years.

The actions are again three: he took, he pressed, he gave. Squeezing fresh grapes straight into a cup compresses the long process of winemaking into a single motion, matching the accelerated growth of the vine. The point of the dream is not how wine was made but that the butler’s service was restored. The cup passes from his hand to Pharaoh’s hand, a picture of renewed trust between master and servant.

That final image of the cup in Pharaoh’s hand is the hopeful detail. The king receives what the servant offers. Nothing intervenes between the work and its acceptance. Set beside the baker’s dream, where birds snatch the food and Pharaoh receives nothing, the difference already hints at the opposite outcomes. Joseph, listening, would have heard both what was said and what was signified. Yet the interpretation he will give is not drawn from clever reading of symbols; it rests on his confidence that God, who sent the dream, would make its meaning known.

wordNotes.explanation: The verb sachat, “to squeeze” or “press out,” occurs only here in the Hebrew Bible. Its meaning is clear from context and from related words in later Hebrew and Aramaic. The rare verb fits the dream’s compressed action, in which grapes go straight from the vine into the king’s cup, and it stands beside the threefold mention of Pharaoh’s cup that the fulfilment repeats (40:21).

verses.bibleText: And Joseph said unto him, This is the interpretation of it: The three branches are three days:

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And Joseph said unto him, This is the interpretation of it: The three branches are three days.” There is no delay, no consulting of manuals, no request for time to deliberate. Joseph answers at once and with certainty. The confidence does not come from Joseph’s cleverness; he has just said that interpretations belong to God, and he speaks as one who has received what he says.

The key he gives is simple: the branches stand for days. The rapid growth of the vine had already suggested that events were near, and the number fixes the span. Joseph may have known that Pharaoh’s birthday fell three days later (v. 20), when royal decisions about prisoners were customarily announced, but knowledge of the calendar could not tell him which man would live and which would die. Only the God who sent the dreams could supply that.

Scripture gives a test for a prophet’s word: if it comes to pass, the LORD has sent him; if not, the prophet has spoken presumptuously (Deuteronomy 18:22). By naming a span of three days, Joseph placed his interpretation where it could be checked almost immediately. That boldness is itself evidence of his faith.

wordNotes.term: זֶה פִּתְרֹנוֹ (zeh pitrono) — this is the interpretation of it
wordNotes.explanation: A formula that introduces the explanation of a dream, repeated for the baker (40:18). Daniel uses the same pattern in Aramaic, “this is the interpretation” (Daniel 4:24; 5:26), when he explains what God has shown the king. The formula signals that the speaker is reporting a fixed meaning, not offering a guess.

verses.bibleText: Yet within three days shall Pharaoh lift up thine head, and restore thee unto thy place: and thou shalt deliver Pharaoh's cup into his hand, after the former manner when thou wast his butler.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“Yet within three days shall Pharaoh lift up thine head, and restore thee unto thy place.” The idiom “lift up the head” comes from the world of the royal court. Subjects bowed low before the king; to have one’s head lifted was to be summoned into his presence and shown favour. The same expression describes the release of King Jehoiachin from his Babylonian prison, when Evil-merodach “did lift up the head” of the captive king and gave him a seat of honour (2 Kings 25:27-28). For the butler, it means pardon and recall.

“And restore thee unto thy place.” The word for “place” is literally “base” or “stand,” the footing on which a thing rests. The butler would be set back on the foundation of his former office. “Thou shalt deliver Pharaoh’s cup into his hand, after the former manner when thou wast his butler.” The interpretation follows the dream detail for detail: the three branches become three days, and the cup placed in Pharaoh’s hand becomes the butler’s renewed service.

The phrase “lift up thine head” carries a further hope in the Psalms. David confesses that the LORD is “the lifter up of mine head” (Psalm 3:3), the one who raises the downcast and restores the disgraced. An earthly king could do this for a servant he chose to pardon. God does it for those who trust him, and in the end he will lift the heads of his people at Christ’s appearing, when Jesus tells them to “look up, and lift up your heads; for your redemption draweth nigh” (Luke 21:28).

The reader should hold this idiom in mind. Joseph will use the identical phrase in a few verses, and its meaning will turn upside down.

wordNotes.term: יִשָּׂא פַרְעֹה אֶת־רֹאשֶׁךָ (yissa’ far‘oh ’et-ro’shekha) — Pharaoh shall lift up thine head
wordNotes.explanation: Nasa’ ro’sh, “to lift the head,” is a court idiom for summoning or honouring someone, used of Jehoiachin’s release (2 Kings 25:27) and of God restoring the humbled (Psalm 3:3). It can also mean to take a census, to count heads (Numbers 1:2). Joseph uses it here for the butler’s restoration, then repeats it with a grim addition for the baker (40:19), and the narrator uses it for both outcomes (40:20).

Ken means a base, stand, or foundation, as with the bronze base of the laver (Exodus 30:18). Applied to a person, it means his office or position. The butler uses the same word when he tells Pharaoh, “me he restored unto mine office” (41:13), recalling how this promise was kept.

verses.bibleText: But think on me when it shall be well with thee, and shew kindness, I pray thee, unto me, and make mention of me unto Pharaoh, and bring me out of this house:

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“But think on me when it shall be well with thee, and shew kindness, I pray thee, unto me, and make mention of me unto Pharaoh, and bring me out of this house.” For the first time in the story, Joseph speaks about himself and asks for something. He has served without complaint and interpreted without payment; now, having given the butler good news, he makes a request in return.

The appeal is carefully built. “Think on me” and “make mention of me” use the same root, the verb to remember, first in its simple sense and then in the sense of causing someone else to remember. Joseph asks the butler to keep him in mind and then to bring him to Pharaoh’s mind. Between those requests stands the word chesed, “kindness,” the loyal love owed within a relationship. The narrator had said that the LORD showed Joseph chesed in the prison (39:21). Now Joseph asks a man to show the same faithfulness. Whether the human friend will prove as loyal as the divine one is the question the chapter leaves hanging.

Joseph’s phrase “when it shall be well with thee” shows his faith in the interpretation. He speaks of the butler’s restoration as certain. He also knows human nature: prosperity is where gratitude is most easily lost. Moses would warn Israel that when they had eaten and were full, they should beware lest they forget the LORD (Deuteronomy 8:10-14). The danger Joseph foresaw is exactly what happened.

Was Joseph wrong to ask? Some have thought his request betrayed a lack of trust in God. The text gives no such hint. Joseph had a just cause, and he sought release through a lawful means that God had placed within reach. Paul later appealed to Caesar to escape an unjust trial (Acts 25:10-11), and prayer for deliverance belongs with willingness to use honest means. Faith does not require passivity. It requires that the outcome be left with God when the means fail, as these did.

Another prisoner, condemned beside Jesus, would one day say, “Lord, remember me when thou comest into thy kingdom” (Luke 23:42). The butler forgot Joseph. Christ forgets no one who calls on him.

wordNotes.term: זְכַרְתַּנִי … וְהִזְכַּרְתַּנִי (zekhartani … vehizkartani) — think on me … make mention of me
wordNotes.explanation: Both verbs come from zakar, “to remember.” The first, in the simple stem, asks the butler to keep Joseph in mind; the second, in the causative stem, asks him to bring Joseph to Pharaoh’s remembrance. In Scripture, remembering is more than recall; it leads to action, as when God “remembered Noah” and caused the waters to recede (8:1). The same pair of ideas returns when the butler says, “I do remember my faults this day” (41:9).

wordNotes.term: וְעָשִׂיתָ־נָּא עִמָּדִי חָסֶד (ve‘asita-nna’ ‘immadi chased) — shew kindness, I pray thee, unto me
wordNotes.explanation: Chesed is loyal, committed kindness, the faithfulness expected of a friend or covenant partner. Abraham asked Abimelech for such kindness (21:23), and Jacob asked it of Joseph regarding his burial (47:29). The particle na’ softens the request into a plea. God’s chesed toward Joseph (39:21) contrasts with the butler’s failure to show it.

verses.bibleText: For indeed I was stolen away out of the land of the Hebrews: and here also have I done nothing that they should put me into the dungeon.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“For indeed I was stolen away out of the land of the Hebrews: and here also have I done nothing that they should put me into the dungeon.” Joseph gives two reasons for his appeal, covering both stages of his misfortune. He did not come to Egypt by any lawful means; he was kidnapped. And in Egypt he had done nothing to deserve prison. Both claims are true, and the reader knows it from chapters 37 and 39.

The Hebrew doubles the verb for emphasis: “stolen, I was stolen.” In the ancient world a person could become a slave through debt or capture in war; kidnapping was a crime, and the law given at Sinai would make it a capital one (Exodus 21:16; Deuteronomy 24:7). Joseph does not name his brothers. He might have told the whole bitter story of their envy and their bargain with the traders. Instead he says only that he was taken by theft. His restraint hints at the forgiving spirit that will later move him to weep over them rather than avenge himself (45:5).

He calls his homeland “the land of the Hebrews.” Canaan had not yet become Israel’s possession, yet Joseph identifies it by his own people, the descendants of Abraham the Hebrew (14:13). Far from home, he has not forgotten who he is or where he belongs.

The word he uses for his place of confinement is bor, “pit” or “cistern,” the same word used for the dry pit into which his brothers had thrown him (37:24). The prison was more than a hole in the ground; Joseph has just called it “this house” (v. 14). Yet to him it was another pit. The repetition connects the two great injustices of his life: first his brothers, then his mistress, had put him down into the depths, though he had done nothing. The psalmist later prays to be kept from going down to the pit (Psalm 28:1), and Jeremiah, cast into a muddy cistern, knew the same terror (Jeremiah 38:6). Joseph’s cry of innocence is the honest appeal of a wronged man, and it anticipates the one who “did no sin” yet was led away to judgment (1 Peter 2:22-23).

wordNotes.term: גֻּנֹּב גֻּנַּבְתִּי (gunnov gunnavti) — indeed I was stolen away
wordNotes.explanation: The infinitive placed before the finite verb intensifies the statement: “I was surely stolen.” Ganav is the ordinary verb for theft, used of Rachel stealing the household gods (31:19) and in the eighth commandment (Exodus 20:15). When the object is a person, the act is kidnapping, which the law punished with death (Exodus 21:16).

A pit or cistern cut into rock to hold water. Empty cisterns served as places of confinement (Jeremiah 38:6; Zechariah 9:11). The same word described the pit Joseph’s brothers threw him into (37:24), so Joseph’s choice of word links his two experiences of being cast down. Pharaoh will later bring him “hastily out of the dungeon” (41:14).

verses.bibleText: When the chief baker saw that the interpretation was good, he said unto Joseph, I also was in my dream, and, behold, I had three white baskets on my head:

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“When the chief baker saw that the interpretation was good, he said unto Joseph, I also was in my dream.” The baker had held back while the butler spoke. Only when he heard a favourable answer did he step forward. His motive was hope rather than trust; he wanted the same kind of news. The words “I also” show that he expected his dream to mirror the butler’s.

The baker’s hesitation contrasts with the butler’s readiness and may reflect a troubled conscience. It also reveals how many people approach God’s word. They are eager to hear it when it promises good and reluctant when it might bring judgment. King Ahab disliked the prophet Micaiah because “he doth not prophesy good concerning me, but evil” (1 Kings 22:8). A true word from God, however, does not adjust itself to the hearer’s wishes.

“And, behold, I had three white baskets on my head.” Egyptian art shows bakers carrying trays and baskets balanced on their heads, so the image belongs to the baker’s daily work just as the vine belonged to the butler’s. Three again sets the timescale. The word translated “white” is uncertain; it may refer to baskets of white bread or fine pastry, or to the pale wicker of the baskets themselves. Either way, the detail places the baker in his familiar role. The dream begins much like the first, and the baker had every reason to expect a happy ending.

wordNotes.explanation: Sal is a basket, the word used for the basket of unleavened bread at the priests’ consecration (Exodus 29:3). Chori occurs only here and is related to a root meaning white or pale; it probably describes white bread or cakes of fine flour, though some take it as wicker. Gideon also carried his offering in a basket (Judges 6:19).

verses.bibleText: And in the uppermost basket there was of all manner of bakemeats for Pharaoh; and the birds did eat them out of the basket upon my head.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And in the uppermost basket there was of all manner of bakemeats for Pharaoh; and the birds did eat them out of the basket upon my head.” The baker’s dream turns where the butler’s did not. The top basket held the finest goods, every kind of baked food intended for the king. Egypt was famous for its bread and pastries, with dozens of varieties listed in its records. All of it was meant for Pharaoh’s table, and none of it reached him.

The birds came down and ate from the basket on the baker’s head, and the baker did nothing. He did not wave them off or protect the king’s food. The contrast with the butler is complete. The butler acted, pressing the grapes and handing the cup to Pharaoh. The baker was passive, and the king received nothing. Abram, when birds of prey descended on his covenant sacrifice, drove them away (15:11). The baker, in his dream, simply let them feed.

The image of birds feeding upon what a man carries on his head was ominous. In the ancient world, to become food for birds was the mark of a shameful death without burial (1 Samuel 17:44; Jeremiah 16:4). The baker may not have grasped this, but Joseph would.

wordNotes.explanation: Literally “food, the work of a baker.” The phrase emphasizes the skill and labour that went into the delicacies meant for Pharaoh. Ma‘aseh, “work” or “product,” is often used for crafted things (Exodus 28:11). The same word ’ofeh names the baker himself (40:1), linking the food to his office.

‘Of is a general word for flying creatures. The birds that eat from the basket become, in the interpretation, the birds that eat the baker’s flesh (40:19). Scripture often pictures exposure to birds as the final disgrace of the dead (Deuteronomy 28:26; Psalm 79:2).

verses.bibleText: And Joseph answered and said, This is the interpretation thereof: The three baskets are three days:

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And Joseph answered and said, This is the interpretation thereof: The three baskets are three days.” The opening is identical to the butler’s interpretation (v. 12). The baker, hearing the same formula and the same span of days, would have felt his hope rise. For a moment the two dreams seem to run in parallel all the way.

Joseph does not soften or delay. He had been glad to bring good news to the butler, and he must now bring the worst possible news to the baker. Faithfulness to God’s word required him to speak it as it was given. Prophets after him faced the same burden: Samuel feared to tell Eli what God had shown him, yet told him everything and hid nothing (1 Samuel 3:15-18). Paul could tell the Ephesian elders that he had not held back anything of God’s counsel (Acts 20:27). A messenger who alters God’s word to please his hearers is no longer God’s messenger, and a kindness that hides the truth is no kindness at all.

wordNotes.explanation: The phrase repeats exactly what Joseph said to the butler (40:12), and the fulfilment comes “the third day” (40:20). Three days is a recurring span in Scripture for a short interval before a decisive outcome, as when Joseph later holds his brothers in custody for three days (42:17).

verses.bibleText: Yet within three days shall Pharaoh lift up thy head from off thee, and shall hang thee on a tree; and the birds shall eat thy flesh from off thee.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“Yet within three days shall Pharaoh lift up thy head from off thee, and shall hang thee on a tree; and the birds shall eat thy flesh from off thee.” Joseph begins with the very words he spoke to the butler, “Pharaoh shall lift up thy head,” and then adds two words that change everything: “from off thee.” The idiom of favour becomes a sentence of death. The butler’s head would be lifted in honour; the baker’s would be lifted from his body.

“And shall hang thee on a tree.” In Egypt, as elsewhere in the ancient world, executed criminals were often displayed on a stake or pole after death, so that their shame was public. Hanging by the neck is not the likely picture here; the sense is of the body exposed on wood. The law of Moses later permitted such display only until evening and declared that “he that is hanged is accursed of God” (Deuteronomy 21:22-23). Paul applies that text to Christ, who became a curse for us when he hung on the tree, so that the blessing of Abraham might come on the nations (Galatians 3:13-14).

“And the birds shall eat thy flesh from off thee.” The dream had shown birds eating from the basket on the baker’s head; the reality would be birds feeding on the baker himself. For Egyptians, who invested heavily in preserving the body and providing a proper tomb, this was an especially dreadful end. The phrase “from off thee” occurs twice, framing the sentence: his head from off him, his flesh from off him.

Joseph speaks with grim clarity. He does not invent a softer meaning or blur the outcome. Scripture does not tell us how the baker reacted, nor does it say what his offence had been. It records only that God’s word through Joseph was exact. Whatever the baker hoped, his future had been shown to him truthfully, and he had three days to face it.

wordNotes.term: יִשָּׂא פַרְעֹה אֶת־רֹאשְׁךָ מֵעָלֶיךָ (yissa’ far‘oh ’et-ro’shekha me‘aleikha) — Pharaoh shall lift up thy head from off thee
wordNotes.explanation: The same idiom used for the butler (40:13) is turned into a play on words by the addition of me‘aleikha, “from upon you.” What was a figure of favour becomes literal removal of the head, or at least the loss of life. The narrator keeps the double meaning when he says Pharaoh lifted up the heads of both men (40:20).

wordNotes.term: וְתָלָה אוֹתְךָ עַל־עֵץ (vetalah ’otekha ‘al-‘ets) — and shall hang thee on a tree
wordNotes.explanation: Talah means to hang or suspend; ‘ets is a tree, pole, or piece of wood. The phrase describes public exposure of a body on a stake, as with the five kings Joshua executed (Joshua 10:26). The law limited such display and called the hanged man accursed (Deuteronomy 21:22-23), a text Paul applies to Christ’s crucifixion (Galatians 3:13).

verses.bibleText: And it came to pass the third day, which was Pharaoh's birthday, that he made a feast unto all his servants: and he lifted up the head of the chief butler and of the chief baker among his servants.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And it came to pass the third day, which was Pharaoh’s birthday, that he made a feast unto all his servants.” The narrator moves straight to the fulfilment. Three days had been foretold, and on the third day the decision came. Pharaoh’s birthday, perhaps the anniversary of his accession as well as of his birth, was an occasion for celebration, and Egyptian texts speak of royal festivals marked by amnesties and the settling of cases. Joseph may have known the date was approaching; he could not have known the verdicts.

“And he lifted up the head of the chief butler and of the chief baker among his servants.” The idiom appears for the third time, now in the narrator’s voice. Both men are brought out before the assembled court, singled out from among the servants. The phrase holds both meanings at once, as Joseph’s interpretations had done. Both heads are “lifted up”; the next two verses will show in what sense.

The third day has an important place in Scripture. On the third day Abraham saw Mount Moriah (22:4); on the third day God came down on Sinai (Exodus 19:11, 16); Hosea speaks of God raising up his people on the third day (Hosea 6:2). Above all, Christ rose on the third day according to the Scriptures (1 Corinthians 15:4). The butler’s restoration should not be pressed into an allegory of resurrection, yet it belongs to a pattern in which the third day brings God’s decisive action after a short time of waiting.

The only other birthday celebration recorded in Scripture is Herod’s, at which John the Baptist was beheaded (Matthew 14:6-10). Both feasts brought death to one man by the will of a king, a reminder of how lightly earthly rulers held life in their hands.

wordNotes.term: יוֹם הֻלֶּדֶת אֶת־פַּרְעֹה (yom hulledet ’et-par‘oh) — Pharaoh’s birthday
wordNotes.explanation: Literally “the day of Pharaoh’s being born,” using a passive form of yalad, “to bear.” The expression may refer to the king’s birthday or to the anniversary of his accession, which Egyptians regarded as a kind of divine birth. The only comparable reference in Scripture is Herod’s birthday feast (Mark 6:21).

From shatah, “to drink,” mishteh is a banquet or drinking feast. Abraham made one when Isaac was weaned (21:8), and Laban made one at Jacob’s wedding (29:22). Fittingly, it is at a feast built around drinking that the cupbearer is restored to serve the king’s cup.

verses.bibleText: And he restored the chief butler unto his butlership again; and he gave the cup into Pharaoh's hand:

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And he restored the chief butler unto his butlership again; and he gave the cup into Pharaoh’s hand.” The fulfilment matches the dream exactly. The butler is reinstated, and the image from his dream becomes literal: the cup passes from his hand into Pharaoh’s hand (v. 11). Joseph’s words had been precise, and the event confirms them to the letter.

The outcome suggests that the inquiry had cleared the butler of whatever charge had been laid against him. Pharaoh not only freed him but entrusted him again with the most intimate service of the court. The man who had looked so sad three mornings earlier now stood at the king’s side.

The verse shows God’s word fulfilled through ordinary political processes. No angel appeared, no miracle was performed in public view. A king held a birthday feast, reviewed the cases of his servants, and made decisions that he thought were his own. Yet those decisions followed precisely the outline God had given through a prisoner three days before. Proverbs says that “the king’s heart is in the hand of the LORD,” turned wherever he will (Proverbs 21:1).

The butler’s return to favour also shows what pardon means. He did nothing to win it while in custody; the king simply chose to restore him. His proper response would have been to extend to others something of the kindness he had received, beginning with the prisoner who had served him and foretold his release. Jesus’ parable of the forgiven servant who refused to forgive his fellow servant turns on the same failure (Matthew 18:32-33), and the chapter’s last verse shows the butler falling into it.

wordNotes.explanation: The noun mashqeh, which in verse 1 meant the cupbearer himself, here means his office or the drink service he provided. The same word can mean drink or the act of giving drink (1 Kings 10:5, where it describes Solomon’s cupbearers and their service). The butler later uses a different word, ken, when he recalls being restored (41:13).

verses.bibleText: But he hanged the chief baker: as Joseph had interpreted to them.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“But he hanged the chief baker: as Joseph had interpreted to them.” The sentence is brief, almost abrupt. No details of the execution are given, no last words, no description of the scene. The narrator simply records that the baker died exactly as Joseph had said. The terse statement carries its own weight.

The closing phrase, “as Joseph had interpreted to them,” is the point. Both outcomes came to pass as foretold. The interpretation was neither vague nor open to adjustment after the fact. Three days, one restoration, one execution: every element was fulfilled. Joseph’s claim that interpretations belong to God (v. 8) was vindicated before witnesses. The butler would recall this precision two years later when he recommended Joseph to Pharaoh: “as he interpreted to us, so it was” (41:13).

For Joseph himself the fulfilment carried a further message. If God had spoken truly through the officers’ dreams, then the dreams God had given Joseph years before, of sheaves and stars bowing down, were also trustworthy. Their fulfilment had not yet come, yet the God who kept his word in three days could keep it over thirteen years. Habakkuk would later say of God’s vision: “though it tarry, wait for it; because it will surely come” (Habakkuk 2:3).

wordNotes.term: כַּאֲשֶׁר פָּתַר לָהֶם יוֹסֵף (ka’asher patar lahem Yosef) — as Joseph had interpreted to them
wordNotes.explanation: The verb patar closes the account of the dreams, matching its use in verse 8, where the officers lamented that there was no one to interpret. The butler repeats this phrase before Pharaoh, “as he interpreted to us, so it was” (41:13). The test of a true prophet’s word is that it comes to pass (Deuteronomy 18:22).

verses.bibleText: Yet did not the chief butler remember Joseph, but forgat him.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“Yet did not the chief butler remember Joseph, but forgat him.” The chapter that began with two men in trouble ends with one man forgotten. Every prediction had been fulfilled; the only request left unfulfilled was Joseph’s own. He had asked the butler to remember him (v. 14), and the narrator says, with deliberate repetition, that the butler did not remember and that he forgot. The doubled statement leaves no room for doubt. Joseph’s hope of release had faded.

The forgetting was more than a lapse of memory. In Scripture, to remember someone means to act on their behalf, and to forget is to neglect. The butler had every opportunity: he stood daily at Pharaoh’s side. Back in comfort, he had no wish to bring up his own time in prison or to plead for a Hebrew slave accused of assaulting his master’s wife. Gratitude cost him something, and he declined to pay. Ecclesiastes tells of a poor wise man who saved a city by his wisdom, “yet no man remembered that same poor man” (Ecclesiastes 9:15). The world often forgets those who help it.

For Joseph, the days stretched into months, and the months into two full years (41:1). There is no record of his words during this time, but the disappointment must have been sharp. The friend who could have helped had turned away. Every human door had closed. It was perhaps the hardest test of all, coming just when hope had been roused.

Yet the butler’s forgetfulness was not the last word. Had the butler spoken at once, Joseph might have been released and sent home or lost in obscurity, with no access to Pharaoh when the king’s dreams came. God’s timing required that Joseph remain in the prison until the very moment when Pharaoh needed an interpreter. What looked like abandonment was God’s careful waiting. The psalmist says that God tested Joseph “until the time that his word came” (Psalm 105:19).

The God who remembered Noah (8:1), Abraham (19:29), and Rachel (30:22) had not forgotten Joseph. He says to his people, “Can a woman forget her sucking child?… yea, they may forget, yet will I not forget thee” (Isaiah 49:15). Those who wait on him will find that his timing, though slow by human reckoning, proves exactly right.

wordNotes.term: וְלֹא־זָכַר … וַיִּשְׁכָּחֵהוּ (velo’-zakhar … vayyishkachehu) — did not remember … but forgat him
wordNotes.explanation: Two verbs express one idea, negatively and positively: the butler did not remember, and he forgot. The repetition is emphatic. Zakar, “to remember,” recalls Joseph’s plea in verse 14; shakach, “to forget,” is often used of Israel forgetting God (Deuteronomy 8:11). God, by contrast, does not forget his people (Isaiah 49:15). The butler finally remembers two years later (41:9).

teachingNotes.openingQuestion: What do you do when the person who could help you forgets you?
teachingNotes.mainPoint: Joseph served faithfully in prison, pointed troubled men to the God who alone reveals the future, and saw God’s word fulfilled exactly, yet he had to keep waiting when human help failed; God’s timing, not human memory, governed his release.
discussionQuestions: What does Joseph’s question, “Wherefore look ye so sadly to day?”, show about the man prison had made him?
Why does Joseph say that interpretations belong to God before he asks to hear the dreams?
How do the two dreams resemble each other, and what details signal that their endings will differ?
Was Joseph wrong to ask the butler for help, and what does his appeal teach about honest requests in hard times?
How might the two-year delay after the butler’s forgetfulness have served God’s purpose for Joseph and for his family?
commonMisunderstandings: Joseph did not claim a personal skill in reading dreams; he credited every interpretation to God (40:8; 41:16).
The chapter does not endorse dream interpretation as a technique; God gave a true word through his servant where the trained interpreters of Egypt had no access.
Asking the butler for help was not a lapse of faith; trusting God and making a just appeal through lawful means belong together.
The butler’s forgetfulness did not mean that God had forgotten Joseph; the delay brought Joseph before Pharaoh at the moment God intended.
teachingNotes.emphasis: Keep verse 8 at the centre. Joseph’s confession that interpretations belong to God shapes the whole chapter, and its exact fulfilment proves that the word came from God. Then let verse 23 teach patient trust: human help failed, but God’s purpose did not.
teachingNotes.closingAppeal: If you feel forgotten in a place you did not choose, serve those around you, speak of the God who holds the future, and trust that he has not forgotten you; his timing will prove right.

evangelisticNotes.mainDoctrinalTheme: God alone knows and reveals the future, and his word is sure; the same God who fulfilled Joseph’s interpretations exactly has given trustworthy prophecy in Scripture and remembers those who wait on him.
flow: Two royal officials in prison had troubling dreams and no one to explain them.
Joseph declared that interpretations belong to God, and God gave him the meaning.
Both interpretations came true on the third day, proving that the word was from God.
God has given prophecy in Scripture so that we can know his purposes and trust his promises.
When people forget us, God remembers; we can wait for his timing and commit our lives to him.
simpleIllustrations: A sealed letter makes sense only when the writer explains it; Joseph knew that the dreams were God’s letters and that only God could open them.
A friend promises to put in a word for you and then never calls; the silence hurts, but the outcome of your life was never in that friend’s hands.
evangelisticNotes.appealQuestion: Will you trust the God who knows the future with your future, even when his timing seems slow?
cautions: Do not present the chapter as a guide to interpreting personal dreams; its point is God’s sovereignty and the trustworthiness of his word.
Do not speculate about the officers’ offence beyond what the text says.
Handle the theme of being forgotten with care, since some listeners carry real wounds from broken promises.

reflectionQuestions: Do I notice the troubled faces around me, even when my own situation is hard?
When I am given insight or success, do I give the credit to God as Joseph did?
Can I make an honest appeal for help without letting bitterness toward those who wronged me take over?
How do I respond when someone I helped forgets me?
Am I willing to wait for God’s timing when the door I hoped for stays shut?
